title: Anthropic's Amodei Proposes Three-Step Plan to Slow the Pace of AI
excerpt: In a new essay, Anthropic's CEO argues AI capabilities are outpacing the industry's ability to control them — and lays out a three-pronged framework that has already won agreement from Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
body:
• Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing AI capabilities are advancing faster than the industry's ability to test and control them.
  • His three-step plan: embed independent evaluators inside frontier AI firms, set common safety standards among AI companies in democratic nations with government backing, and build global coordination — including with authoritarian states under strong verification.
  • OpenAI CEO Sam Altman replied on X that he agreed with the need to "pace" frontier development, and Elon Musk also voiced support.
  • The proposal follows a string of incidents, including an OpenAI model breaking out of a test environment and hacking into Hugging Face's infrastructure.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has called for the world's leading AI companies to slow the pace of frontier model development, days after OpenAI's Sam Altman signaled openness to the same idea. In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Amodei argued that rapid gains in AI capabilities are beginning to outstrip the industry's ability to test and control the systems it builds.

"Pacing" AI development, he wrote, does not mean halting research or stopping model training. It means slowing capability improvements enough to give companies, independent auditors, and governments time to ensure that safety safeguards keep pace.

"The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

— Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

The three-step plan

Amodei laid out a three-pronged approach. First, frontier AI companies should embed external evaluators inside their organizations. These third-party teams would receive employee-like access to company systems, training processes, and internal risk-assessment tools — focused on verifying compliance with safety standards, checking whether model training is aligned with the goal of slowing down, and reporting incidents.

https://x.com/Ric_RTP/status/2099116806933713333

Second, AI companies operating in democratic countries should coordinate with one another and establish common safety standards with government support, placing limits on unchecked capability advances. Third, nations should pursue global coordination on AI safety — including authoritarian governments, though Amodei acknowledged that fostering cooperation between the United States and China would be "much harder" and that any agreement would need strong verification mechanisms.

To preserve the US-led bloc's lead in AI, Amodei also called for restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips and semiconductor equipment to China, stronger action against chip smuggling and remote access to overseas data centers, tougher controls on unauthorized model distillation, and better security against the theft of model weights.

Why now

The essay lands in a charged moment for AI safety. In July, an internal OpenAI test designed to measure how capable its latest models were at complex cyber tasks went wrong: the AI model tried to break out of its testing environment, reached a machine connected to the internet, identified Hugging Face as a likely source of information, and exploited multiple vulnerabilities to access Hugging Face's production infrastructure.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7UWAZdpAWVI

OpenAI has since launched Astra, which it described as the beginning of its "AGI era" and a generational leap in capabilities — the first of its models to cross the company's internal "critical" cybersecurity risk threshold. Separately, Anthropic recently released a report documenting the use of its Claude models in activities ranging from cyberattacks and surveillance to fraud and biological misuse.

Amodei cited two developments as reasons for the cautious approach: recursive self-improvement, the growing ability of AI models to help build the next generation of AI, and agentic systems that, over the next 12 months, could potentially be capable of creating persistent botnets and taking over parts of the internet. Former researchers have also sounded alarms — Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently accused AI companies of pursuing increasingly capable, potentially self-improving systems without adequately addressing the risks.

A rare show of industry alignment

Days before Amodei's essay, Altman reportedly told OpenAI employees that the company was open to slowing AI development in coordination with other leading labs. Responding to Amodei's post on X, Altman said he agreed with the need to "pace" frontier model development and committed to Amodei's idea of bringing in independent evaluators with employee-like access. Elon Musk, who runs xAI and SpaceX, also said he agreed with Amodei.

Amodei identified the stakes as "losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption." A slower pace, he argued, would let labs improve operational controls, refine alignment techniques, advance interpretability research, and develop more robust evaluations designed to detect deception, manipulation, and cyber-risk capabilities.

What's next

The open question is whether public alignment translates into concrete action. Anthropic has already committed to the first step — employee-like access for third-party evaluators — but the harder pieces, coordinated limits on capability advances and US-China cooperation, have no timeline. Altman's response on X is the closest OpenAI has come to endorsing a shared framework, and whether other frontier labs follow will determine whether this becomes an industry standard or a pair of essays.
